extracted.intended_audience: general public, students and practitioners of public health/medicine
extracted.subtask_description: Practical preventive and management guidance for common infectious diseases (typhoid, scarlet fever, measles, whooping cough, chicken pox) including water and food hygiene, well construction, quarantine, disinfection, and symptomatic treatment. Geared toward reducing transmission in households and communities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid or sterilize drinking water when infection is possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Where any possibility of the infection of drinking water occurs, that water ought either to be avoided or else to be thoroughly sterilized before using.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies particularly to old-fashioned wells with loose board covers and chain pumps. Examples: epidemics traced to contaminated river tributaries, shallow wells near privies, and wells contaminated by leeching from nearby privies. Anti-pattern: relying on a cover or shallow depth alone without sterilization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well construction: watertight lining and cover
rubrics_metrics.description: Two points essential if well water is to be kept pure: (1) line the well with a water-tight masonry lining, and (2) have the cover of the well made with a thoroughly water-tight coating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This may still fail if polluting matter passes through soil or rock cracks. Examples: an iron-cased well contaminated via a crack in laminated granite despite a 25-foot casing. Masonry lining and watertight covers are necessary but not always sufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well siting: avoid fissured/laminated rock and nearby privy vaults; sand/gravel safer
rubrics_metrics.description: Wells in fissured or seamed rock and in limestone are especially dangerous if pollution exists nearby; pollution may follow rock surfaces horizontally a long distance. In sand or fine gravel the danger of contamination is almost negligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a well reaches a horizontal layer of limestone and a privy vault is dug to the same rock, contamination frequently occurs. Long Island example: wells and cesspools ten to fifteen feet deep and only fifty feet apart showed no contamination in sand/gravel. Anti-pattern: siting wells near privies or on fissured/laminated rock.

rubrics_metrics.name: Milk hygiene: prevent post-milking contamination
rubrics_metrics.description: Milk becomes infected only after it is drawn from the cow, typically because infected water is added, cans are washed in contaminated water, or infected handlers touch milk or utensils.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sterilize milk cans and bottles; do not reuse bottles without sterilizing. Examples: Somerville 1892 (milkman with typhoid son), Stamford 1895 (milk washed with polluted water leading to 386 cases), Montclair 1902 (bottles contaminated at a house on route). Anti-patterns: washing cans in polluted water or failing to sterilize returned bottles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control and exclusion of flies to prevent transmission
rubrics_metrics.description: Flies transmit typhoid because they are born in and frequent filth; they carry material on their feet and can deposit germs wherever they alight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevent fly breeding by excluding privies, cesspools, manure and garbage from fly access. Evidence: experiment with a fly walking on a gelatine plate grew millions of bacteria. Historical examples: Spanish–American War outbreaks attributed largely to flies; Japanese army success attributed to active fly control measures. Anti-pattern: neglecting fly breeding sites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid consumption of raw shellfish and produce washed in contaminated water
rubrics_metrics.description: Oysters fattened in sewage-polluted water can contain typhoid germs inside the shell; lettuce and celery washed in contaminated water or handled by unclean hands or fertilized with manure may transmit disease.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not eat raw oysters from suspect sources; ensure produce is washed with clean water and handled hygienically. Example: oystermen fatten oysters in dirty water to speed 'plumping up' — a risk factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent direct-contact transmission by strict hand and food hygiene
rubrics_metrics.description: Transmission may occur by direct contact when caregivers soil their hands and then infect themselves by touching mouth or handling food/dishes; giving partly consumed food from a sick person to children is risky.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid sharing dishes or food from sick persons with healthy individuals; caregivers should practice hand hygiene and avoid feeding the child food used by the patient. Anti-pattern: using the same handkerchief/dishes for sick and well without disinfection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment principle for typhoid: supportive care and avoidance of harmful interventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Typhoid is best treated by being let alone with moderate modification: rest, hydration, careful nursing, baths, and proper diet; no drug is of any avail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incubation ~10 days; provide plenty of water, sponge baths or tub baths (temperatures may be low), and nourishing but easily digested liquids like milk and eggs. Avoid exposure, fatigue, and injudicious feeding which can cause relapse or digestive complications. Emphasize 'uninterrupted watchful care' rather than aggressive drug therapy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antitoxin/testing for typhoid is experimental; prioritize sanitation and care
rubrics_metrics.description: Although some army officers report an antitoxin for typhoid and inoculated soldiers, results are inconclusive; the writer believes education and preventing escape of germs from sick rooms and careful food/drink handling are the primary hope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely solely on experimental inoculations; continue sanitary measures, food and drink care, and household infection control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quarantine for scarlet fever: strict isolation during peeling and at least one week after last sign
rubrics_metrics.description: During the process of peeling (desquamation) contagion seems most active; the patient should remain strictly isolated during this time and at least a week after the last sign disappears.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peeling often lasts two to five weeks. Keep the child at home, possibly on a porch with moderate exposure, until safe to reintroduce. Rationale: contagion may be carried on skin scales and clothing; historical cases show clothing packed away long after an illness causing new infections years later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thorough disinfection after scarlet fever
rubrics_metrics.description: To prevent transmission after apparent recovery, thorough disinfection should be practiced: the patient's body covered with antiseptic ointment, sick room disinfected, and bedding steamed or boiled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wash all surfaces with carbolic acid solution 1 in 50 or corrosive sublimate 1 in 1000. Steam or boil bedding; clean clothing and utensils. Rationale: contagion may persist on clothing and in trunks/bundles for long periods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measles management: isolation, ventilation, rest, and local antiseptics
rubrics_metrics.description: Physicians keep measles patients in bed, insist on abundant ventilation, and recommend sponge baths, nourishing easily digested food, and antiseptic sprays for nose and throat and carbolized vaseline for skin when peeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shield patient from drafts and avoid eye use (reading/close work) to protect eyes. Prevent exposure that leads to lung complications; disinfect dishes and clothing via boiling/steaming and wash walls and room surfaces after vacancy. Rationale: early stages resemble common cold so early isolation reduces spread.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stamp out epidemics early to prevent increased severity
rubrics_metrics.description: As an epidemic progresses, the disease (e.g., scarlet fever) may become more serious and death-rates may rise; therefore strong efforts ought to be made to stamp out an epidemic while it is in the first stages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early isolation, thorough disinfection, and public-health measures reduce the chance that a relatively low fatality rate will escalate during a prolonged epidemic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whooping cough: isolate once cough starts; protect caregivers and disinfect belongings
rubrics_metrics.description: Whooping cough is likely not contagious until the cough starts; the child should be isolated as soon as the first whoop occurs and kept until the last whoop has passed. The nurse should protect against spreading infection after leaving the sick room.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a big apron with long sleeves fitted closely around the neck that can be slipped on/off easily as protection. Disinfect dishes, napkins, towels, handkerchiefs, and bedding by boiling or steaming. Provide fresh air, moderate exercise, good food, and a mild nerve depressant if needed. Avoid sending symptomatic children to school.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chicken pox: symptomatic care, antiseptic ointments, and avoid scarring
rubrics_metrics.description: Chicken pox is mild in children; use antiseptic ointment (e.g., carbolized vaseline) to avoid irritation and prevent scratching which may leave deep scars. Contagion is apparently airborne and short-lived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adults with suspected chicken pox should be quarantined as smallpox suspects. Less extensive surface disinfection is typically practiced compared with scarlet fever or measles. Rationale: pustules progress in successive crops and are readily recognizable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disinfect clothing, dishes, and room surfaces from sick rooms before reuse
rubrics_metrics.description: All dishes and clothing of every sort should be boiled or steamed and soaked in a disinfecting solution before removal from the sick room; the room itself should be disinfected and walls washed after vacancy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific solutions: carbolic acid 1 in 50 or corrosive sublimate 1 in 1000 for scarlet fever; general practice is boiling/steaming for fabrics. Anti-pattern: removing or reusing bedding/clothing without adequate disinfection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect eyes and avoid exertion during convalescence of eruptive diseases
rubrics_metrics.description: In scarlet fever and measles the eyes are apt to be affected; it is important to keep the patient in a darkened room and to forbid use of the eyes in reading or other close work until recovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also avoid exposure and overexertion during recovery to prevent lung complications and other after effects. Rationale: complications frequently follow exposure during convalescence.
